content.title: When could Cade Cunningham return from collapsed lung? Explaining the timeline
content.text: The Detroit Pistons’ loss of All-Star Cade Cunningham to a collapsed lung could threaten the team’s final playoff push and Cunningham’s individual award odds.Cunningham is due to be re-evaluated in two weeks, the team announced Thursday, but a full recovery may require further rest and rehabilitation. As it stands, he will miss at least the next eight games, more than half of the 14 regular-season matchups left on Detroit’s schedule.Collapsed lungs can result from a wide variety of injuries, such as puncture wounds and complications during medical procedures. Numerous pro athletes have dealt with collapsed lungs in recent years because of errors while undergoing dry-needling, which involves using thin needles to release tightened muscle trigger points and relieve pain. Dry-needling is legal in 37 states and Washington D.C., and it’s become commonplace in pro sports. Players such as Pittsburgh Steelers edge rusher TJ Watt and quarterback Tyrod Taylor, currently a free agent, have suffered collapsed lungs because of needle punctures.The much more common situation involves direct trauma. That appears to be Cunningham’s case, as his injury occurred after a blunt force impact he suffered on Wednesday while diving for a loose ball during the Pistons’ game against the Washington Wizards.Cunningham fell into the legs of Wizards rookie Tre Johnson five minutes into the game, causing Johnson to go airborne and crash onto Cunningham’s side. Johnson’s elbow hit Cunningham’s lower back and right hip on the way down, and Detroit’s 24-year-old star immediately winced in pain before slowly sitting up. He left the game with what the Pistons described as back spasms, but an evaluation later revealed a collapsed lung. When he returns will depend on an array of factors. Cade Cunningham won’t return tonight due to back spasms. This is the play that took him out pic.twitter.com/Mj5ZHcWL7G — Pistons Talk (@Pistons__Talk) March 17, 2026Recovery times varyDetroit’s two-week re-evaluation timeline fits the typical treatment for a collapsed lung, known medically as a traumatic pneumothorax. People generally need to rest for several days to let their lungs inflate again and feel relief from their symptoms. Once they cross that threshold, it could take another week or two to resume normal physical activity.“Two weeks is the mark that we look at, including (factors) like resumption of activity or air travel,” said Dr. Emily DuComb, a pulmonary disease specialist at the University of Michigan. “However, if there was any other sustained damage or if there are structural lung issues, sometimes that can be a longer process that would need ongoing reevaluation.”Playing basketball at an elite NBA level is not a “normal” activity, though. There’s also the extensive travel involved in NBA life, which can impact lung health. In two weeks, Cunningham’s doctors will look to make sure his lungs are recovering as normal, then give him a better idea of when he can return to the court. He could need a few extra days, or he could need another couple of weeks. He could be ready to go immediately. It just depends on the person and any outlying factors.Dr. DuComb said in Cunningham’s case, given the strenuousness of professional basketball, it wouldn’t be “unreasonable that it may take a little longer to get up to the level of physical activity that he’s typically able to do.”The Pistons’ announcement didn’t indicate Cunningham suffered any fractures during the collision, which likely rules out the possibility that a broken rib poked a hole in the lung. Instead, the pressure from Johnson’s fall itself most likely compressed Cunningham’s lung with enough force to burst part of the organ’s outer wall.This is where individual physiology comes into play. Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum, for instance, has suffered two lung collapses in his career, one in 2021 and another in 2023. McCollum was able to return from the first in about six weeks, while the second recovery period lasted less than a month. Cunningham’s recovery could go either way.“Most of the time, because people have healthy lung tissue and intrathoracic structures, we would expect recovery in one to two weeks,” Dr. DeComb said.Due to HIPAA, we may never get all the details on what Cunningham’s specific case is unless he decides to share his medical information for some reason. That said, while uncommon overall, most collapsed lungs have similar root causes.Excess air builds upSome people are particularly at risk of collapsed lungs because they have small growths called blebs along the outside of their lungs. These blister-like pockets of air are normal and don’t impact a person’s health unless they rupture. We don’t know if that’s what happened to Cunningham, but tall, young men like him are most vulnerable to developing blebs and suffering collapsed lungs, Dr. DeComb said.“I don’t know if we know exactly why they’re more prone to developing them, or if it’s more just an association that we’ve identified,” she said. “But it certainly can be a contributor.”In the event of a rupture, the air inside the blebs is released into the chest and creates internal pressure, which is the reason some patients experience immediate shortness of breath and pain. That isn’t always the case, and Dr. DeComb said collapsed lungs can go undiagnosed depending on the amount of air released.“If a small amount builds up, patients won’t have a ton of symptoms. But if a lot of air builds up, that can lead to significant symptoms and, in some cases, be catastrophic,” she said. “Otherwise healthy adults, if they don’t have that amount of air building up and creating kind of that collapse, can really handle these very well.”Doctors can perform various treatments to remove the excess air, such as inserting a needle or tube into the affected area and siphoning it out. But in most cases, the lungs will reabsorb the air on their own as they heal.Detroit is atop the Eastern Conference standings, but losing Cunningham leaves the Pistons in a rough spot. He is averaging 24.5 points, 9.9 assists, 5.6 rebounds and 1.5 steals per game this season, and it’s unlikely anyone on the Pistons can make up for those contributions. Plus, the Pistons are already without keystone center Isaiah Stewart, who’s nursing a left calf strain and will be re-evaluated on Tuesday.The good news is that Cunningham’s injury should have a relatively straightforward recovery outlook. The bad news is that the NBA season is nearing its end, and every game matters from here on out.
